source.title: Recovery and Generalization in Over-Realized Dictionary Learning
source.authors: Jeremias Sulam; Chong You; Zhi-Hui Zhu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It reports dictionary-learning test-risk results across model sizes and training-set sizes, a different setting and method from the deep-network double-descent claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites work on neural-network generalization and over-parameterization, but those cited results are not this study's results. The study's own relevant outcomes are the dictionary-size sweep in Figure 1a, the training-set-size results in Figure 1c, and the risk curves in Figure 2b. Figure 4 and Appendix C compare parameter settings or algorithms after distillation to the original dictionary size, so they do not provide separate model-size risk sweeps. Several plotted values are not numerically recoverable from the text.
record.test_reason: Figure 1a sweeps dictionary size from 70 to 500 atoms and reports test risk. This is a model-size risk curve in a non-deep model class (sparse dictionary learning), a new setting that bears on V4. The paper does not frame it as double descent. It reports a fall then a rise, which it calls 'well understood' overfitting, and no second descent within the tested range.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. The authors conclude that over-realized dictionaries lower training and population risk within some range and improve recovery of the ground truth. They show that usage-based distillation yields an original-size dictionary with consistently better recovery across parameters and algorithms (ODL+OMP, ODL+Lasso, K-SVD), and that the benefit degrades smoothly with noise. They attribute the eventual rise in test error to insufficient training data, a behaviour they call well understood statistically. They leave the optimal over-realization degree and the mechanism (possibly optimization-landscape related) open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses dictionary learning with ODL or K-SVD and sparse-coding methods, not the original deep-network scaling and test-error measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports benefits across dictionary parameters and learning algorithms. It also reports that the recovery benefit of over-realization deteriorates smoothly as added Gaussian noise increases.
record.problems: The relevant risk curves are largely presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The sample-size results do not specify the direction of the effect or identify a near-interpolation condition. The dictionary-size experiment does not establish a later second descent.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were extracted from Figure 4 or Appendices C: these compare parameter settings or algorithms after distillation to the original dictionary size, rather than reporting distinct test-risk sweeps by evaluated model size.

untested.parts: No test error over training epochs is reported.
Figure 1c varies sample size, but the text gives no direction of the effect near an interpolation threshold.
It is not tested whether a second descent appears beyond p′=500 or at larger over-parameterization relative to n.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
The noise experiment (Figure 5a) measures recovery improvement only, not a risk peak or its removal by regularization.
No recounting of complexity is done.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is changed from T2 to T3: this is a different model class (a new setting) rather than a different method aimed at the same question. The study is not about double descent. It is relevant only because Figure 1a gives a size-vs-test-risk curve past the point of perfectly fitting the training data, and that curve shows no second descent. All relevant values are figure-only. Figure 5b reports a 'phase transition' in minimal atom usage at p′=70, but that is an optimization statistic, not risk.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns dictionary learning, not deep networks.
It does not measure test error over training epochs.
The sample-size sweep does not identify an interpolation threshold or explicitly report whether increasing samples near that threshold raises test error.
The study does not locate an interpolation threshold or demonstrate a later second descent after the reported increase in test risk.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The noise experiment concerns recovery improvement, not whether noise or regularization causes, splits, or removes a risk peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective parameter measure or test whether that changes a double-descent curve.

rows.subject: ODL [Mairal et al., 2010] with OMP for sparse coding
rows.size_stated: Estimated dictionary size p′ ranges from 70 to 500; ground-truth dictionary has 70 atoms and size 50 × 70.
rows.operation_detail: Varied estimated dictionary size and measured test risk.
rows.uncertainty: Mean over 20 repetitions with 25% and 75% percentiles
rows.note: The text says test error improves as dictionary size increases over some range, then generalization error increases as the training set becomes insufficient for the larger model, while training data are perfectly fit. It does not report a later decline in test error.
rows.check: State is defensible. Test error falls, then rises while the training data are perfectly fit, and no later decline is reported up to p′=500 with n=300. The initial fall begins at the ground-truth size (70), not in a classical under-parameterized regime. The interpolation point is never located numerically.

source_check.correct: state=absent for V4: test risk initially improves with dictionary size, then increases while training data are perfectly fit; no renewed descent is reported in the tested range.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Figure 1a and accompanying experimental description; discussion immediately before Section 3.1.
source_check.problem: The initial improvement does not establish partial post-interpolation descent; the reported perfect-fit regime instead has increasing generalization error.

rows.subject: ODL [Mairal et al., 2010] with OMP for sparse coding

rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured test risk.

rows.note: The text states that test generalization error is controlled by training-set size, but does not describe whether more samples raise or lower it. The plotted values are not stated numerically in the text.

rows.subject: ODL [Mairal et al., 2010] with OMP for sparse coding, over-realized dictionary
rows.size_stated: Estimated dictionary size p′ ranges from 80 to 140; ground-truth dictionary has 70 atoms.

rows.note: This is the over-realized test-error curve in the comparison with the distilled dictionary. The text describes the figure mainly in terms of recovery error and does not state the test-error trend numerically or in prose.
rows.check: The range p′=80–140 with n=500 is narrow. The text gives no test-error trend in prose, so the row cannot show a second descent.

rows.subject: ODL [Mairal et al., 2010] with OMP for sparse coding, distilled dictionary
rows.size_stated: The distilled dictionary has the original size of 70 atoms; the over-realized dictionary size varies from 80 to 140.
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error after distilling an over-realized dictionary to the original size.
rows.note: This measures the distilled dictionary's test error as the size of the model it came from varies; the evaluated dictionary itself remains at the original size. The paper does not describe the plotted test-error trend in prose.
rows.check: The distilled dictionary is evaluated at a fixed size (70 atoms). This compares the study's own distillation method, not test risk against evaluated model size, so it bears on no version.

relationships.condition: ODL+OMP dictionary learning, d=50, true p=70, k=3, n=300, p′ from 70 to 500
relationships.reason: R1: test risk falls, then rises while training data are perfectly fit, with no second descent reported in the tested range. In this model class the post-interpolation regime looks like classical overfitting, though the range may be too short to rule out a later descent.
relationships.display_finding: Test risk initially fell and then rose while training data remained perfectly fit, with no renewed descent over the tested dictionary sizes.
